item.title: Clued-in | From 'China Shock' to 'China Squeeze': 'China threat' narrative falls apart
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Clued-in | From 'China Shock' to 'China Squeeze': 'China threat' narrative falls apart China's economy has delivered a strong performance in the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), with its GDP expanding 4.7 percent and total goods trade surging 16.9 percent year on year. Yet the more impressive China's economic performance becomes, the more reluctant some quarters appear to acknowledge it. In the global discourse surrounding China's development, narratives have been repeatedly repackaged, from "China Shock 1.0" to "China Shock 2.0" and now to the so-called "China Squeeze." These narratives all serve the same purpose: portraying China's development achievements as "abnormal" and providing a pretext for protectionist policies. Increasingly, voices around the world are exposing the flaws in these narratives, and the view that China's development creates opportunities rather than squeezes others is gaining wider recognition. 'China Shock 1.0': A one-sided reading of economic history In an article titled "The Myth of the China Shock" published on the website of Project Syndicate on Aug. 18, Michael R. Strain, director of economic policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, argues that the "China Shock 1.0" narrative oversimplified the complex economic adjustments brought about by trade liberalization, reducing them to a cause-and-effect story that blamed U.S. job losses on Chinese exports. A screenshot of the article "The Myth of the China Shock" published on the website of Project Syndicate. The "China Shock 1.0" argument claims that competition from Chinese imports between 1990 and 2007 contributed to the loss of around 1.5 million manufacturing jobs in the U.S. Yet Strain argues that this interpretation presents only one side of the trade story. During the same period, the expansion of U.S. exports created nearly as many jobs, meaning that the effects of trade were not simply a one-way loss caused by imports. He also argues that the "China Shock 1.0" narrative ignores longer-term structural trends in the U.S. economy. Manufacturing's share of total U.S. employment had already been declining since the early 1950s, decades before the so-called "China Shock." China, however, has often been used as a convenient scapegoat for broader changes in the U.S. industrial structure. As Strain writes, every part of the "China Shock" narrative is "off base." 'China Shock 2.0': Framing competition as 'overcapacity' "China Shock 2.0" shifts the focus from labor-intensive sectors to advanced manufacturing, including electric vehicles, batteries and solar energy. It portrays normal industrial competition as "unfair" and frames China's scale advantages as evidence of "overcapacity." Jostein Hauge, a political economist and assistant professor in development studies at the University of Cambridge, has highlighted the double standards behind such accusations. When China uses industrial policies to build manufacturing capabilities, they are often portrayed as unfair. When the U.S. adopts similar measures, such as those under the $280 billion CHIPS and Science Act, they are generally viewed as legitimate policy tools. An article titled "The Costs of Keeping China Out," published on the website of Foreign Affairs on Aug. 17, warns of the risks of shielding U.S. companies from Chinese competition. A screenshot of the Foreign Affairs article "The Costs of Keeping China Out" by Peter Cowhey, a professor at the University of California San Diego, and Meg Rithmire, a professor at Harvard Business School. The authors, Peter Cowhey, a professor at the University of California San Diego, and Meg Rithmire, a professor at Harvard Business School, argue that blocking Chinese products such as electric vehicles may protect U.S. companies in the short term, but also prevents them from facing stronger competition and catching up with the technological frontier. "Chinese firms are no longer merely efficient producers or copycats; in terms of knowledge and production capability, they are increasingly global leaders in many industries," the authors write. "Denying them access to the American market harms U.S. competitiveness, hinders U.S. efforts to build industrial capacity at home, and ensures that U.S. industry and consumers remain far from the frontier of technological advancement." They also suggest that the U.S. should learn from China's development experience, adopting a strategy of selective openness that "permits carefully structured Chinese investment in areas in which the economic and technological benefits are substantial while imposing stringent safeguards to mitigate security risks." A screenshot of the opening of the Foreign Affairs article "The Costs of Keeping China Out." "There is a clear precedent for this strategy," they write. "It is, in fact, exactly what China did to Western companies for decades." 'China Squeeze': A narrative built on counterfactual assumptions The latest "China Squeeze" argument extends a debate rooted in Western economic anxieties to the Global South. Put forward by some Indian economists, it holds that if China had not industrialized, countries such as India and those in sub-Saharan Africa would have had greater opportunities to develop low-skilled manufacturing industries. However, Adam Tooze, a historian at Columbia University, challenges this logic in an article on Substack, describing it as a form of counterfactual speculation. According to Tooze, development is not a queue; it is not so much a process as a project. "Each such project is more or less well adjusted to its context," he writes. A screenshot of a Substack article by Adam Tooze, a historian at Columbia University, challenging the logic of the "China Squeeze" narrative. Another scholar, Leon Liao, identifies three major flaws in the logic of the "China Squeeze" narrative in a lengthy Substack article titled "The Myth of the China Squeeze: Part I." First, it rests on flawed counterfactual reasoning. The argument assumes that if China exported less, developing countries would automatically export more. But a shirt no longer produced in China would not necessarily be made in the poorest countries. Orders could move to other manufacturing hubs, shift to highly automated producers elsewhere, or disappear altogether as higher costs push up prices. Second, it mistakes market share for "squeezing" others. The argument treats market share won through Chinese industrial competitiveness as an excessive claim on global development space, effectively turning industrial success into evidence that China is crowding out other countries. But gaining market share through competition does not by itself mean that China is preventing others from developing. Third, it treats industrialization as a predetermined sequence. The argument presents postwar industrialization as a relay race in which advanced economies withdraw from lower-skill manufacturing and pass the baton to later developers. Yet, as Liao writes, the "flying-geese" model does not establish a general obligation for successful economies to abandon industries in which they remain competitive. The U.S. did not withdraw from agriculture or aerospace after becoming rich; Germany did not abandon automobiles, machinery or chemicals; and Japan and South Korea retain major positions in steel, shipbuilding and other industrial sectors, according to Liao. "There is no historical formula for how much industry China 'should' abandon," Liao writes. A screenshot of a Substack article by Leon Liao titled "The Myth of the China Squeeze: Part I." The evolution from "China Shock 1.0" to "China Shock 2.0" and then to "China Squeeze" reveals a consistent pattern: whenever Chinese industries make breakthroughs in a new field, a new accusation is leveled against China, recasting its competitiveness as somehow illegitimate. The political function of these narratives remains unchanged: providing domestic legitimacy for protectionism while seeking international sympathy. The facts point in the opposite direction. China has emerged as an anchor of stability in the global economy. In the first half of 2026, China's imports reached 10.74 trillion yuan ($1.6 trillion), up 22.1 percent year on year. China has granted zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries, South-South trade has grown tenfold over the past three decades, and Chinese companies' investments and manufacturing operations in Southeast Asia have helped strengthen local supply chains. All of this shows that China's development is creating demand, transferring technology and generating new growth opportunities rather than crowding other economies out. Whether labeled "China Shock" or "China Squeeze," these narratives share the same fundamental mistake: treating competitiveness itself as a problem while blaming one's own lack of competitiveness on the efforts of others. China's development has never been a shock to the world. It has been more like a fast-moving train offering opportunities to those willing to get on board. The choice between joining the competition and retreating behind protectionist walls will determine who comes out ahead. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Smart lighting makes the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge greener
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Smart lighting makes the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge greener Photo shows the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge in Wuhan, central China's Hubei province. (Photo/Zhang Heng) The Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge, located in Wuhan, central China's Hubei province, is hailed as the "First Bridge over the Yangtze River." It holds deep collective memories for generations of local residents. When night falls, the bridge glows with soft, warm-yellow lights, forming an iconic part of Wuhan's nighttime cityscape. Wan Quan, now 52, has been driving for over three decades. Once a taxi driver, he now works for a company that operates engineering vehicles. A frequent commuter between the two riverbanks of the Yangtze, he has witnessed the steady emergence of river-crossing bridges across Wuhan. He has also witnessed significant changes in the lighting of these bridges over the years. "In the early days, the bridge lights were quite dim, with low brightness and limited coverage. I had to be especially careful whenever driving at night," Wan recalled. Today, LED lights make driving across the bridges safer and more comfortable, providing brighter, more even illumination, a clear view and lower energy consumption. When the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge opened to traffic in 1957, it was lit by 512 spherical lanterns fitted with 60-watt incandescent bulbs. In the 1970s, all light sources were replaced with 80- to 125-watt high-pressure mercury lamps. At the beginning of this century, the entire bridge was equipped with 250-watt high-pressure sodium lamps, creating the iconic orange-yellow glow that became a signature of Wuhan's nightscape. "Sodium‑vapour lamps appear bright, but their light is harsh and offers poor color rendering. Road surface colors and lane markings become hard to distinguish. Prolonged night driving often left drivers with sore, dry eyes," explained Chen Junyu, director of the industry technical review section at the streetlight management and service center of Wuhan Power Supply Company. Chen also noted that humidity is high over the Yangtze River. During rainy or foggy weather, light from fixtures without precision optical lenses scatters easily, creating a hazy curtain of light that can obstruct drivers' vision and compromise road safety. An even more pressing issue was energy consumption. High-pressure sodium lamps have relatively low photoelectric conversion efficiency, and at the time, smart lighting controls were not available. Regardless of weather or traffic conditions, the lights were switched on and off at fixed times and operated at a constant brightness. Hundreds of lamps on the bridge consumed large amounts of electricity, while prolonged operation at high temperatures accelerated aging and increased failure rate. In recent years, guided by China's carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals, phasing out energy-intensive lighting equipment has become an inevitable step. The challenge for urban management is to strike a balance between preserving iconic nighttime landscapes and achieving greener, smarter, and more energy-efficient lighting. "With continued technological advances, LED light sources have made significant improvements in key indicators of light quality, including luminous efficacy and color rendering. This has made it possible to deploy energy-efficient lighting on a much larger scale," Chen said. Since the beginning of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), Wuhan has been comprehensively advancing its urban green lighting program, gradually replacing metal halide and sodium lamps, which have relatively low luminous efficacy and high energy consumption, with energy-efficient LEDs. The city has also promoted the installation of individual-lamp control systems. Combined with Internet of Things communications technology, these systems allow each lamp to be dimmed independently and enable road illumination to be precisely adjusted according to different time periods and road sections, improving energy saving and extending lamp life. In November 2025, the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge began an upgrade of its lighting system. The existing 150 units of 250-watt high-pressure sodium lamps were replaced with 200-watt LED ones, supported by a smart control system that enables time-based dimming. Before the upgrade, the bridge consumed 450 kilowatt-hours of electricity per day. After the upgrade, daily consumption fell to 144 kilowatt-hours, representing an overall energy saving rate of 68 percent, equivalent to an estimated annual saving of about 110,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity. "The new streetlights have fully preserved the bridge's iconic nighttime appearance while effectively addressing problems such as harsh glare," Chen said. More importantly, the new LED fixtures combine high luminous efficacy, low energy consumption and a long service life, delivering substantially greater energy savings than traditional high-pressure sodium lamps. After dinner, Chen visited a smart lighting management and control office at the streetlight management and services center. A large screen displayed basic data on transformers, lamp posts, lights and cable lengths across the city, as well as maps showing how streetlights are connected to different circuits. "With this smart lighting management and control office, we can control individual lamps, adjust brightness according to different time periods, and provide lighting as needed, enabling more targeted energy saving," said data analyst Peng Jingjing. Peng clicked on the circuit serving the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge on the map. The screen immediately displayed the dimming strategy for 70 LED lights along that road section, along with the resulting energy savings. The lights are no longer switched on and off at fixed times; instead, their operating schedules are determined according to outdoor light levels. So far, five river-crossing bridges in Wuhan have completed installation or upgrading of LED lighting systems along their entire length. By the end of 2027, all of them are expected to be equipped with smart lighting systems. The approach will also be rolled out across the city. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: International journalists witness China's rescue efforts in mudslide-ravaged Gyirong
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
International journalists witness China's rescue efforts in mudslide-ravaged Gyirong GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Even with prior knowledge of the catastrophe, Brazilian journalist Bruno Falci Bitarelli Medeiros was struck by the harsh rescue conditions after a bumpy 12-hour bus ride from Lhasa to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. The final stretch wound through rugged mountain roads, unpredictable weather and falling rocks. "It's a very difficult condition for the workers, and I very much admired how they keep searching for people," Medeiros said. Medeiros was among a group of journalists from international media outlets including CNN, Reuters and NBC who visited the devastated port from Saturday to Sunday. A press conference attended by domestic and foreign journalists is held in Gyirong County, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida) At a media briefing by the local emergency rescue headquarters, they heard from technical experts and local officials about ongoing efforts on multiple fronts: the search for the missing, victim identification, community assistance and secondary disaster prevention. The fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port in Xigaze City on the China-Nepal border on Aug. 26. As of 6 p.m. on Sept. 5, 43 people were confirmed dead and 519 remained missing. SEARCH GOING ON At the core disaster zone, a 35-meter-high flood mark, roughly the height of a 12-story building, was scored into the cliff above the ruins. "Everything below the flood mark was originally underwater," said Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters and acting mayor of Xigaze City. "Power was gone. What you see now is what we've restored in the past couple of days." Rescuers conduct search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida) Land access to the port was restored on the morning of Sept. 2, allowing heavy machinery to move in and clear working areas. Mud deposits average four meters deep in the hardest-hit zone, with some areas reaching 16 meters. Inside the core area, vehicles and machinery are conducting deep-search operations -- excavating, searching and clearing layer by layer during grid-by-grid sweeps. Konda Jagan Mohan Varma from the Press Trust of India watched the operation. "The glacier breakdown brought down a lot of slush, mud and huge rocks together," he said. "A large part of infrastructure was damaged on both sides, in China and Nepal." He noted the scale of the rescue effort unfolding around him -- heavy machinery carving through the debris, teams fanning out across the ruins in methodical searches. Just an hour after the journalists arrived, the valley turned from sunshine to pounding rain, forcing an emergency evacuation. Rescuers have persisted in such conditions for more than 10 days. As of 6 p.m. on Sept. 5, China had deployed over 2,500 rescue personnel, more than 500 vehicle trips and over 9,000 sets of search equipment, and air-dropped more than 5 tonnes of supplies. Two people from a nearby village have been rescued, and nearly 1,000 personal items have been recovered. BEYOND BORDERS After repeated verification, authorities confirmed that 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries, including Nepal, India, Latvia, the United States and Britain, remain missing. For identification, each body is numbered, photographed and sampled for DNA and dental records at the scene. The headquarters has set up a dedicated identification team. So far, none of the bodies retrieved are foreign nationals. Rescuers work at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida) Responding to a question about the identification process for the missing, Yang Lahong, deputy director of the foreign affairs office of Xizang, said at the briefing that the names and specific information of missing foreigners have not been made public to protect their privacy, but have been shared with the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels. A 24-hour hotline for families of missing foreign nationals has received 509 calls, with feedback provided promptly, Yang added. At Nepal's request, the Chinese government has dispatched tunnel rescue and DNA testing experts to Nepal, along with emergency material assistance. Through a China-Nepal disaster prevention information notification mechanism, daily updates on meteorology, hydrology, glacial lakes and glaciers are shared with Nepal. After the disaster, many Nepalese border residents were stranded in China due to the port closure. Local authorities have seen to the daily needs of 1,720 Nepalese border residents. Green channels for foreign personnel entry and exit have been opened. A total of 3,388 foreign nationals originally planning to leave via Gyirong Port have been diverted, and authorities have helped 365 Nepalese border residents cross the border to return home. WATCHING FOR NEXT DANGER Preventing secondary disasters remains a priority. More than 170 experts and technicians are now monitoring the area with over 150 sets of equipment, including slope radar and drones. Along the main rescue route, 58 geological hazard spots have been identified, seven of them high-risk. Rescuers use a laser-based AI monitoring device to dynamically monitor risks such as landslides and falling rocks at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong County, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Jigme Dorje) Hu Bo, leader of the China Anneng rescue detection team, serves as a "sentinel" for frontline workers. When upstream data showed abnormal movement, he sounded the retreat signal. Whistles echoed through the gorge as personnel and machinery pulled back to safety zones. Hu said such scenarios can happen several times a night. Muhammad Asghar from the Associated Press of Pakistan observed the monitoring efforts. "The monitoring for secondary disasters is being done tirelessly, day and night," he said. On the site, Medeiros spotted civilian drones flying to observe potential risks for a secondary disaster. "The technology today is being very helpful to rescue operations in this disaster," he said. "Some countries use drones for war, but China uses drones to help people." Medeiros noted that, as global warming is the root cause of the disaster, more concrete actions from the world are needed to prevent these kinds of disasters from happening again, citing China's push for a green economy as an example. Asghar agreed. "Climate change is not the issue of only one country. The whole world should put their heads together," he said. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China to reinvent centuries-old industries with heritage and AI
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
China to reinvent centuries-old industries with heritage and AI BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China on Monday unveiled its first national policy document for silk, tea, porcelain and other centuries-old industries, as part of efforts to leverage the country's rich cultural heritage and build strong global brands. By 2028, the country aims to cultivate 50 enterprises with annual revenues exceeding 10 billion yuan (about 1.48 billion U.S. dollars) each, Xie Yuansheng, vice minister of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), told a news conference. The document also calls for 100 Chinese consumer brands and several industrial clusters with annual output exceeding 100 billion yuan to be developed by 2028, he added. By 2030, these industries are expected to produce a group of world-class enterprises and renowned brands, while moving toward the mid- to high-end of the global value chain, according to the document issued by the MIIT and five other government departments. In addition to the industries mentioned above, the document also covers traditional Chinese medicine, brewing, arts and crafts, and the "four treasures of the study" -- writing brush, ink stick, paper and inkstone -- all deeply rooted in Chinese culture and traditions dating back centuries or even millennia. Representative sectors of these traditional industries boast about 25,000 enterprises above the designated size, employing nearly 3.5 million people and generating about 8 trillion yuan in annual revenue, according to Xie. Historically, these products traveled along ancient trade routes as far as Central Asia, the Mediterranean and even Africa, carrying Chinese craftsmanship and culture far beyond the country's borders. In recent years, the appeal of Chinese culture overseas has continued to rise. Content creators around the world are making aspects of Chinese culture part of their daily lives -- from drinking hot water and wearing slippers around the house to eating Chinese food and wearing red. The document also comes as China seeks to translate its rich cultural heritage into greater market competitiveness. About 90 percent of China's silk products are exported, but mainly as raw materials or original equipment manufacturer goods, with domestic brands having limited pricing power in the global market, said Feng Haicang, an official with the MIIT's consumer goods industry department. "Our challenge is to make sure these time-honored crafts are not only admired but also commercially successful, and to restore these historic Chinese products to their rightful place at the high end of international markets," said Feng. China will hold the first national exposition of time-honored industries in east China's Hangzhou City in late October, Xie said. AI is expected to play an important part in boosting these industries, according to the document. The technology will be used to digitize traditional craft knowledge, decode traditional production processes and improve efficiency and product quality on factory floors. In silk weaving, AI-assisted design can now generate thousands of patterns in minutes, said Xie. A DEEP POOL OF CRAFT KNOWLEDGE These industries draw strength from China's vast intangible cultural heritage, which provides a deep reservoir of craft knowledge, skills and cultural creativity for their continued development, said Shan Gangxin, an official with the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, at the news conference. Traditional arts, crafts and medicine, Shan noted, share deep roots with industries like silk, tea and porcelain, and have evolved alongside them. China now has 45 elements inscribed on UNESCO's lists and register of intangible cultural heritage, including silk craftsmanship, acupuncture and tea-processing techniques. More than 100,000 items are also recognized on national, provincial, prefectural and county-level intangible cultural heritage lists. In July, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. The country's large pool of skilled practitioners is also a solid base for industrial development. More than 200 universities have taken part in training programs for intangible cultural heritage practitioners over the past decade, benefiting more than 200,000 heritage inheritors, said Shan. The economic potential of traditional skills is already clear in the way they have been adapted to today's markets. Willow weaving in Linyi, east China's Shandong Province, for example, has evolved from a craft once best known for making baskets and hampers into a wide range of contemporary products, from stylish cultural and creative products to playful items such as cat climbing frames. The industry now has more than 300 patents and over 20,000 product designs, with its products reaching more than 80 countries and regions, according to Shan. Traditional craftsmanship is also finding new channels and audiences. This summer, creative products featuring hemp weaving, Huzhou writing brushes and Zhuang brocade were officially licensed for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. By the end of 2025, China had 14,900 intangible cultural heritage workshops, supporting employment and higher incomes for more than 1.3 million people, Shan said. item.title: AI-powered "Made in China" sharpens global appeal in tech hub
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
AI-powered "Made in China" sharpens global appeal in tech hub SHENZHEN, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Inside a flagship store of Chinese drone maker DJI in the city of Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, British visitor Annabel Grainger was busy taking photos of products to share with her friends back home. "My friends wouldn't have seen anything like that before," she said. A thriving tech hub, Shenzhen has emerged as a magnet for global tech aficionados. The city's wide range of high-tech products, including artificial intelligence (AI) glasses, AI 3D printers, AI robots, drones, and handheld gimbal cameras, have generated considerable buzz on international social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok. An average of nearly 8,000 foreign buyers visit Huaqiangbei, Shenzhen's mega electronics marketplace, each day this year. From January through July, sales of AI products surged more than 55 percent from a year earlier in this area. Sales of AI glasses doubled, while sales of drones and robots climbed by 60 to 70 percent during the same period. Industry insiders noted that a complete industrial chain and high-density industrial clusters have taken shape in Huaqiangbei's AI sector, covering the full spectrum from AI chip solutions and agent development to on-device model deployment and scenario testing. These advantages, they said, have facilitated the deep integration of AI technologies into hardware products, while boosting production efficiency and significantly lowering costs. "It takes several weeks to make a prototype in Europe, but it can be done in half a day in Shenzhen," Dutch engineer Henk Werner said. "In Shenzhen, if you need to upgrade a product, you can pull together all your suppliers within a day and have a cooperation agreement inked by the evening," said Leng Xiaokun, founder of Leju Robotics, highlighting the city's core advantage in having a complete industrial chain. The company's Kuafu line of humanoid robots has, notably, achieved a domestic sourcing rate of 95 percent for its core components, which has significantly reduced costs and enabled rapid market launch. In a bid to incentivize enterprises to double down on fundamental core technologies over the long haul, Nanshan District in the city, home to a vibrant tech ecosystem, has set up a seed fund and an angel fund totaling 500 million yuan (approximately 73.7 million U.S. dollars), aimed at offering lead investment support to early-stage ventures. "Though the research and development of the fundamental components and algorithms of humanoid robots often yields no direct returns for several years, Shenzhen's patient capital provides a guarantee for technological breakthroughs," Leng noted. Leveraging an international cooperation center based in the city's Longhua District, a host of advanced technology firms have successfully introduced their AI-powered intelligent computing terminals and other smart products and solutions to markets across North America and Southeast Asia. Shenzhen has also jointly built cooperation platforms with ASEAN member states. The Shenzhen-Singapore cross-border data verification platform, now in trial operation, is designed to address challenges related to secure data flows in AI and other industries. Adjacent to Hong Kong, Shenzhen was one of China's first special economic zones and has since evolved, over four decades, into a global hub for innovation and advanced manufacturing. The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, while the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of almost 30 percent. Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, an industry research report said. item.title: AI to take center stage at 5th global digital expo
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
AI to take center stage at 5th global digital expo People visit the 4th Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 25, 2025. (Xinhua/Jiang Han) BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The 5th Global Digital Trade Expo, an event dedicated to promoting digital trade and industrial cooperation, will take place from Sept. 23 to 27 in Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province, with artificial intelligence (AI) as its main theme, an official said on Monday. More than one-third of the exhibitors will focus on AI, alongside the collective debut of AI application pilot bases, presenting a full-chain innovation ecosystem spanning foundational models, industry applications and smart devices, China's Vice Minister of Commerce Yan Dong noted. A number of AI competitions will be held on the sidelines of the expo, covering areas such as open-source development, embodied intelligence and brain-computer interface technology. The expo will feature 170,000 square meters of exhibition space, with international exhibitors accounting for over 20 percent of the total. The number of overseas pavilions has already exceeded the combined total of all previous editions. Malaysia and Hungary will be the guest countries of honor, while representatives from 121 countries and regions and 29 international organizations have confirmed their attendance. The expo has so far attracted nearly 40,000 professional buyers, including more than 12,000 from overseas, with expected international procurement orders reaching 977 million U.S. dollars. China's digitally deliverable service trade value expanded at an average annual rate of 11.2 percent between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global average by 1.8 percentage points. According to a guideline on boosting reform and innovative development of digital trade released in November 2024, China expects the share of digitally deliverable service trade in total service trade to exceed 45 percent by 2029 and 50 percent by 2035. The Ministry of Commerce will work with other government departments to implement the guideline, support local governments in tailoring policies to boost digital trade, and foster a coordinated effort to advance the sector, Yan added. item.title: Wildlife thrives in nature reserve in NW China's Xinjiang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Wildlife thrives in nature reserve in NW China's Xinjiang Photo shows a vibrant autumn view of Ganjiahu saxaul national nature reserve in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. (People's Daily Online/Yang Rui) The Ganjiahu saxaul national nature reserve in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region is teeming with lush vegetation and increasing numbers of wildlife spotted across its desert landscape. Thanks to continued conservation efforts focused on ecological restoration as well as regular patrols and monitoring, the nature reserve features abundant water resources, well-connected waterways, and a stable wetland water area. Wild saxaul trees, desert poplars, and tamarisks have expanded across the reserve, boosting vegetation cover and helping stabilize the desert landscape. The improving ecosystem has also benefited the local wildlife. Infrared cameras have frequently captured rare animals moving through the forest, including goitered gazelles, red foxes and elks, while both water birds and migratory birds have been seen resting and foraging in the wetlands. Photo shows a vibrant autumn view of Ganjiahu saxaul national nature reserve in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. (People's Daily Online/Yang Rui) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Interview: China's services fair opens new doors in the "marketplace of ideas," says economist
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Interview: China's services fair opens new doors in the "marketplace of ideas," says economist This photo taken on Sept. 2, 2026 shows a view of the Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu) JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) is an important platform for economies and businesses to explore new opportunities in the services trade as knowledge and data become increasingly important drivers of global growth, a South African economist has said. "CIFTIS will increasingly move beyond being simply an exhibition and become a marketplace for ideas, technology, investment and international partnerships," Simphiwe Madikizela, professor of economics at the University of South Africa, told Xinhua in a recent interview. The 2026 CIFTIS will be held from Sept. 9 to 13 in Beijing, bringing together exhibitors from over 90 countries and international organizations, along with more than 1,800 companies. Madikizela said the fair's theme, "Global Services, Shared Prosperity," is particularly relevant as the global economy shifts from a model dominated by trade in manufacturing goods toward one increasingly driven by services, technology and intellectual property. China's rapidly growing services trade provides an important example of this transformation, he said, citing data that China's trade in services increased by 8.3 percent year-on-year to nearly 3.78 trillion yuan (about 556.56 billion U.S. dollars) in the first half of 2026. "China's services trade is increasingly moving toward higher-value activities," said Madikizela, noting that knowledge-intensive services trade reached 1.66 trillion yuan, accounting for 44 percent of total services trade, and grew 6.7 percent in the first half of the year, while exports of such services rose 12.8 percent. Such development is significant not only for China but also for the global economy, as the world's second-largest economy is becoming not only a major producer of goods but also an increasingly important market and provider of services, he added. Visitors watch the exhibition "This is the Shang" with MR devices at the Cultural & Tourism Services exhibition area of the 2025 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 12, 2025. (Xinhua/Xu Qin) Highlighting China's vast domestic market and demand, the economist said, "An open Chinese economy can support global growth through trade, investment, tourism, digital services, professional services, technology and innovation." "At a time when geopolitical tensions and protectionism are creating uncertainty, greater cooperation in services can provide another channel through which economies remain connected," Madikizela said, adding that against this backdrop, CIFTIS can play an important role in strengthening international services cooperation. CIFTIS reflects a broader transformation in globalization since international economic integration is no longer simply about moving physical products across borders, but increasingly about the exchange of knowledge, technology, skills, data and services, he said. Madikizela added that the development of China's services trade is contributing to what he described as the "servicification of global trade," as manufacturing and services become increasingly integrated. For developing economies, particularly in Africa, CIFTIS offers opportunities to connect with Chinese and international partners in areas such as digital trade, e-commerce, financial services, tourism, education, healthcare, logistics and professional services, he said. "The future will not be defined only by how many containers cross international borders but by how effectively countries exchange services, technology, knowledge, data, skills and innovation," Madikizela said. "That is why initiatives such as CIFTIS are becoming increasingly important to the global economy." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China's foreign trade maintains rapid growth in first eight months
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
China's foreign trade maintains rapid growth in first eight months BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained swift growth in the first eight months of 2026, with both exports and imports posting solid gains, and import growth continuing to outpace exports, official data showed on Tuesday. The country's total goods imports and exports rose 17.6 percent year on year to 34.78 trillion yuan (about 5.13 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-August period, according to the General Administration of Customs. The growth rate was 0.3 percentage point faster than that recorded in the first seven months of the year. Exports increased 14.6 percent year on year to 20.17 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22 percent to 14.61 trillion yuan, the data revealed. In August alone, China's goods trade totaled 4.65 trillion yuan, up 19.8 percent from a year earlier and remaining above the 4-trillion-yuan mark for a sixth consecutive month. Exports grew 18.6 percent year on year in August, while imports rose by 21.7 percent. Both exports and imports registered double-digit growth for a fourth straight month, and import growth exceeded that of exports for a sixth successive month. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online.
